Here we’ve got a nice lemon-lime yogurt blend with a touch of candy sweetness, wrapped in a creamy vanilla blanket. It leans more on Lime than the lemon, despite the ratios being the same, but without that lemon it’s more of a Key Lime Pie taste than that distinct 7-Up-esque tartness.

Key with this one being the marzipan, which throws in a sweet candy note in there - even half a percent is more than enough to get the note in there - anything more than 0.5% and you’re looking at a whole different beast - it’s going to fight the Yogurt notes and smother them. The recipe minus the marzipan is decent enough on it’s own.

Optional - add a drop per 15ml Koolada to give it a slight smack of cool. I tend to double that ratio of Koolada for my mints, but it’s really distracting at that ratio with this recipe. Halve it - one per 15 or even 20mls. Gonna want that one slight with this recipe - it’s not a ‘cool’ recipe, rather a recipe that benefits from a small amount of ‘cool’ in it.

Enjoy!

2% - FA Lemon Sicily

2% - FA Lime (Cold Pressed)

3.5% - FA Yogurt

2.5% - TFA Greek Yogurt

1.5% - TFA Vanilla Bean Ice Cream

1% - FA Fresh Cream

0.5% - FA Marzipan

Optional - 1 drop Koolada per 15ml

I just finished listening to “Dreaming in Code” by Scott Rosenburg on Audible. The book was recommended to me as a ‘great learning experience for building applications’. This recommendation probably needs to be amended to ‘how not to build applications’ for accuracy. The book makes me sad and a little bit angry. I want to vent after reading this book. This is my rant.

Don’t read this book expecting to learn how to be a better developer. But if you are new to programming you probably should read this book for the ‘what not to do’ project management lessons. Take this book as a historical account of a project train wreck. Learn from these mistakes. It will give you a better understanding of why startups like to run engineering sprints.

For those of you unfamiliar with that term, engineering sprints are scheduled around delivering a certain set of features at the end of a time period. The engineers break down these features (also called user stories) into discrete bits of work (this is called grooming). Typically it’s the amount of work developers feel comfortable they can code and test in a 2 week timeframe. (I’ve greatly simplified the whole Agile model for the sake of brevity).

I found the interviews about Agile programming processes humorous. It almost seems like the author sought out only the opinions of detractors. And they turn out to be misguided. I have the luxury of working under a modified Agile methodology with a ‘launch then iterate” philosophy. Making product decisions, building features and releasing them is much more fun than the alternative.

Joel Spolsky wrote a good review of the book on his blog at http://www.joelonsoftware.com/items/2007/01/21.html. He saved me the time of detailing of some of the big fat blind spots of the Chandler team, spending years and millions of dollars. How frustrating would it have been to work on this project? You spend a lot of time in meetings rehashing topics you’ve already covered, revisiting decisions that were already made, rewrite a lot of code and then release little. “Dreaming in Code” is too good a title for this book. A more accurate title would have been “Meetings, No Code”.

If you are new to programming, you might miss that the author mixes two different kind of application development projects. He is comparing apples (internal IT projects) with oranges (product development) when he cites software project failure statistics.

Internal IT projects are considered a ‘cost’ to the business. The products the business develops are consider ‘revenue generating’ and are less likely to be shelved.

IT projects constantly have to justify why they are needed. These kinds of projects are more likely to ‘fail’ as a cost cutting measure or because a business might decide to throw bodies at a problem instead of software. The end users are employees so the development process is less likely to include the same kind of competitive analysis and market research as does a product a company markets for sale. There are no revenue numbers to track or marketshare to acquire.

The author fails to make this distinction and doesn’t recognize that part of the inefficiency of Chandler project might be because it didn’t need external revenue to keep going. If they needed to generate revenue or encourage user donations, there may have been a greater sense of urgency to get design decisions finalized and turned into product.

The title includes the phrase “4,732 bugs”. Really? Bugs against what? Features that only exist in the minds of the developers? The ‘flicker’ bug gets mentioned and seems a legitimate bug. I failed to believe the project had this many bugs given the churn over the application architecture and user interface. What specs were they testing against? How do they verify and validate the bug exists? I wish the book spent more time explaining the nature of these bugs and how they were reported.

The author mentions the addition of a designer to the team and how the developer wants to push back and ignore her work based on his mental model of how the user will behave. Nowadays, engineers will route some traffic to one interface (A) and route other traffic to a second interface (B) and then compare to see which user interface has the best user metrics. There is no way to know if the UI design is on the right track without testing it with real users. The developer is too close to the project and not a good proxy for an end user. A/B testing wasn’t a thing yet, so it’s unfair of me to expect the author to discuss it.

A/B testing is something you should make yourself familiar with if you want to get into web development professionally. Etsy once spent 6 months on a feature that users ignored. Now they design small specific tests to help validate UI changes. Read more here http://apptimize.com/blog/2014/01/etsy-continuous-innovation-ab-testing/.

The main fault I had with the book is the how it promotes itself as a book that ‘uncovers the mystery of why writing code is so hard’. This implies the book will tell us is how teams write code. A better statement is “how the Chandler project chose to make writing code so hard”.

For example, the Chandler team debated coding for the browser and using AJAX (process the user request immediately in a web page, no need to reload the whole page) and chose not to pursue these technologies. It’s not clear how the author missed the emergence of companies that embraced these technologies and were delivering innovation in reasonable timeframes.

Salesforce.com made $178M in 2005 with their web-based Sales Automation application. Other companies embraced AJAX during this timeframe, Kayak.com and Microsoft Exchange in 2003 and Gmail in 2004. (Note: by the time his book was published, Google will launch Google Apps (a suite of products that included Gmail, Google Talk and Google Calendar). This product suite will make Google $1B in 2012.)

The struggle was real for the Chandler project. The project objectives were very grand and the tools available were not up to the need. This book is not a ‘why writing code is hard’ guide, it is a snapshot in the computing history timeline. This is before the adoption of Agile methodologies and Extreme programming. This is before Ruby on Rails and Software as a Service became common. This was before programmers collaborated with Github. A better description of this book for me is “why writing code WAS harder and here is what not to do in the future”.

End of rant. Do I recommend reading this? If you have high blood pressure, maybe not. Otherwise it’s worth the read to learn what not to do.
